note: Ohio has something rare and worth knowing about: a Youth and Family Ombudsmen Office that takes complaints directly from young people, with a separate form for youth and for families. Most state oversight assumes an adult is doing the reporting. Ohio's child abuse line is also a directory rather than a call centre - it connects you to the county office that will actually handle it.

civil_injury.summary: One year for assault, battery or false imprisonment. Two years for other bodily injury claims, such as negligence (for example, a program that failed to protect you).
civil_injury.quote: an action for assault or battery shall be brought within one year after the cause of the action accrues.
civil_injury.note: 2305.10(A) (https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-2305.10): 'an action for bodily injury ... shall be brought within two years after the cause of action accrues.' 2305.11(A) (https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-2305.11): false imprisonment 'shall be commenced within one year after the cause of action accrued.' Under 2305.111(B), if the victim did not know who the attacker was, the assault/battery claim accrues when the identity was learned or reasonably should have been. Section 2305.111 current version effective March 21, 2025.

civil_minor_tolling.summary: If you were under 18 when you were hurt, the clock does not start until you turn 18. So assault or battery claims are due by your 19th birthday, and negligence claims by your 20th.
civil_minor_tolling.quote: if a person entitled to bring any action mentioned in those sections, unless for penalty or forfeiture, is, at the time the cause of action accrues, within the age of minority or of unsound mind, the person may bring it within the respective times limited by those sections, after the disability ...
civil_minor_tolling.note: Applies to sections 2305.04 to 2305.14, which covers 2305.10, 2305.11 and 2305.111. No cap on the tolling. No general discovery rule or extended period for non-sexual child abuse was found; the 12-year childhood sexual abuse period in 2305.111(C) is sexual-abuse only and out of scope here.

civil_government_claims.summary: Claims against the State of Ohio go to the Court of Claims within two years (or a shorter period if one applies, such as one year for assault); claims against a county, city or other local government must be filed within two years, paused while the victim is a minor.
civil_government_claims.quote: shall be brought within two years after the cause of action accrues, or within any applicable shorter period of time for bringing the action provided by the Revised Code. The period of limitation contained in this division shall be tolled pursuant to section 2305.16 of the Revised Code.
civil_government_claims.note: 2743.16(A) (https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-2743.16): state claims 'shall be commenced no later than two years after the date of accrual' or any shorter period applicable to similar suits between private parties. No separate pre-suit notice-of-claim requirement was found in these sections. Whether 2305.16 minority tolling applies to Court of Claims actions was not confirmed; political subdivision (2744.04) tolling is explicit. Immunity rules in Chapter 2744 may bar many claims regardless of timing.

criminal_child_abuse.summary: Six years for a felony. For crimes that injured a child in a way that suggests abuse or neglect, the six years do not start until the victim turns 18 or until a children services agency or police officer is told about the abuse, whichever comes first.
criminal_child_abuse.quote: shall not begin to run until either of the following occurs: (1) The victim of the offense reaches the age of majority. (2) A public children services agency, or a municipal or county peace officer ... has been notified that abuse or neglect is known, suspected, or believed to have occurred.
criminal_child_abuse.note: Subsection (J) applies to offenses involving a 'physical or mental wound, injury, disability, or condition of a nature that reasonably indicates abuse or neglect of a child under eighteen years of age.' Important: a report to children services or police while the victim is still a minor can start the clock early. Misdemeanor child endangering: 2 years. Section current version effective April 9, 2025.

criminal_felony_assault.summary: Six years for felony assault. Misdemeanor assault must be charged within two years.
criminal_felony_assault.quote: For a felony, six years; For a misdemeanor other than a minor misdemeanor, two years; For a minor misdemeanor, six months.
criminal_felony_assault.note: No limit for aggravated murder and murder (2901.13(A)(2)). 2901.13(A)(3) sets 20 years for listed offenses including kidnapping (2905.01) and felony assault under 2903.13, and for felonious or aggravated assault (2903.11, 2903.12) only when the victim is a peace officer; otherwise felonious assault is under the six-year rule. Failure of a mandated reporter to report child abuse (2151.421) has four years (2901.13(A)(6)). Other subsections of 2901.13 (not quoted) can pause the clock, for example while the offender is out of state.

channels.name: Ohio Counselor, Social Worker and Marriage and Family Therapist Board
channels.what_it_can_do: Licenses and disciplines counselors, social workers and marriage and family therapists in Ohio, and investigates complaints including incompetent practice, breaking confidentiality, failure to tell clients the nature and extent of services, sexual harassment, discrimination, physical or verbal abuse and conflict of interest.
channels.who_to_report: A licensed counselor, social worker or marriage and family therapist in Ohio. Psychologists have their own board.
channels.how: File through the Board's eLicense complaint portal, or download the form and fax it.

channels.name: Ohio State Board of Psychology
channels.what_it_can_do: Licenses and disciplines psychologists and school psychologists in Ohio, and publishes how its investigation process works alongside its complaint form.
channels.how: Use the Board's complaint page, which sets out the investigation process as well as the form.

channels.name: Ohio Department of Behavioral Health
channels.what_it_can_do: Licenses and certifies behavioral health providers in Ohio, including residential treatment, and takes complaints about the services they give.
channels.who_to_report: A certified or licensed behavioral health provider or residential program.
channels.note: Formerly the Ohio Department of Mental Health and Addiction Services (OhioMHAS); the old mha.ohio.gov address now redirects here.

channels.name: Ohio child abuse and neglect reporting line
channels.what_it_can_do: An automated directory that connects you straight to the child welfare or law enforcement office in the relevant county, which is where the report is actually handled.
channels.who_to_report: A child at an Ohio program. Report to the county the program is in.

channels.name: Ohio Youth and Family Ombudsmen Office
channels.what_it_can_do: An independent office for anyone concerned about the Ohio children services system. It takes complaints directly from young people, with a separate route for youth and for families.
channels.who_to_report: A young person in the Ohio system who wants to complain themselves, or a family who has hit a wall with an agency.
channels.how: Use the Youth complaint form or the Family complaint form on the office's site.

channels.name: Disability Rights Ohio
channels.what_it_can_do: Ohio's Protection and Advocacy agency, with federal authority to investigate abuse and neglect of people with disabilities in facilities, a right of access to them, and free legal advocacy.
channels.who_to_report: An Ohio program where the young person has a disability or a mental health diagnosis.
